sessions.title: Generation and Transformation
sessions.description: Highlight formatting, summarizing, translating, and style-shifting competencies across varied text modalities.
sessions.sessionOutline:
This session marks the transition from how AI models function internally to what they can actually achieve for us, focusing on the twin engines of productivity: Generation and Transformation. As a whiteboard-style session, we begin by drawing two main columns on the board. On the left, we write 'Source Material (Input),' and on the other, 'Target Output.' We explain to the students that at its core, text generation is not magic; it is a highly controlled translation of entropy (randomness or a prompt) into organized structure. We address the common misconception that models only 'write new things from scratch' by showing that their greatest production utility lies in converting existing unstructured language into highly formatted, structured modalities.

Next, the whiteboard comes alive with a specific workflow mapping: 'Style-Shifting.' We draw a arrow representing a prompt that acts as a cognitive lens. We write a dry, overly technical paragraph of medical data on the left, and show how a style-shifting instruction acts as a filter, outputting a compassionate patient summary on the right. This demonstrates that translation is not merely switching between English and Spanish, but shifting between 'dialects of intent'—such as turning engineering jargon into executive summaries or casual emails into formal project proposals. We caution teachers to warn students here against 'lazy prompting,' where they ask the model to 'rewrite this' without specifying the audience, tone, or structural constraints, which usually results in generic, bloated corporate-speak.

Moving to the practical component, we sketch out a real-world scenario on the whiteboard: transforming raw structural reports into standardized business formats. We guide the students through a live framing of translation instructions. The teacher should write a prompt template on the board, pointing out the explicit placeholders for 'Context,' 'Tone,' and 'Formatting Rules (e.g., Markdown headers, bullet points).' This visual scaffolding helps students understand that control over generative outputs is achieved by limiting the model's choices rather than letting it wander freely.

We conclude the session with an interactive practice run. Students are challenged to design a set of instructions that takes a chaotic, multi-page technical report and outputs a 3-sentence summary alongside a JSON block of key metrics. By forcing students to design both the input structure and the target output constraint, we reveal a key learning insight: the more structured your input and the more explicit your output format requirements, the more reliable and hallucination-free the model's transformation will be.

tasks: Design translation instructions and style transformations for structural reports.

sessions.title: Classification and Pattern Recognition
sessions.description: Leverage models for lightning-fast scanning, sorting semantic patterns, classification tasks, and high-volume parsing.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome back. Today we are transitioning from creative generation to one of the most powerful, high-volume capabilities of modern language models: semantic classification and pattern recognition. In classical machine learning, getting a computer to sort unstructured text into specific categories required training custom classifiers with hundreds of labeled examples, tokenizers, and rigid feature engineering. Large Language Models (LLMs) turn this paradigm on its head by understanding the underlying concepts and intent immediately. As an instructor, you should begin this session by drawing a stark contrast on your whiteboard: on the left, show a rigid, keyword-matching sorting machine that fails when someone uses a synonym; on the right, sketch an LLM that reads between the lines, grouping diverse emotional feedback into operational categories effortlessly.

Let us illustrate this using a real-world scenario of high-volume customer feedback parsing. If a user writes, 'Your delivery arrived late, but the package was in pristine condition and the delivery person was incredibly polite,' a simple keyword system gets confused. It sees 'late' (negative) alongside 'pristine' and 'polite' (positive). An LLM, however, can run a semantic scan. It recognizes that this feedback contains two distinct signals: a logistics complaint (shipping delay) and a customer service compliment (staff behavior). On the whiteboard, map this out by showing the raw feedback text passing through a semantic 'prism' that splits the input into multi-dimensional vectors. Point out that the model isn't just counting words; it is placing the sentiment of this text in a multi-dimensional mathematical space where 'late delivery' naturally clusters closer to 'Logistics Bottleneck' than 'Product Defects'.

Now, address a major learner misconception: the idea that LLMs will always guess the right category out of thin air. Left to their own devices, models are highly creative and will invent new category names on the fly—one day outputting 'Shipping Delay', and the next outputting 'Logistics Lag'. To prevent this chaos, we must use instruction parameters to constrain the model's output space. Show the students how to construct a robust 'Classification Guardrail' prompt on the whiteboard. Write out the structural components: a clear persona ('You are an expert operations analyst'), a defined input, a strict taxonomy of categories, and—most importantly—the explicit instruction to *only* output the exact category name with zero additional conversational filler like 'Sure, here is the category...'. This prevents downstream parsing failures when automating workflows.

Let us transition into an active practice moment. Have the students design a prompt that categorizes user reviews for a grocery app into three precise operational buckets: 'Inventory' (out of stock), 'Quality' (spoiled or damaged items), and 'App UX' (technical glitches). A common trap students fall into during this exercise is forgetting to tell the model what to do with ambiguous or multi-issue reviews, such as 'The app crashed while I was looking for fresh apples.' Guide them to refine their instructions to establish priority rules (e.g., 'If a technical issue is mentioned, classify as App UX first'). Explain to the students that by defining these logical boundary lines, they are effectively programming a highly flexible cognitive router that can process thousands of reviews in seconds with near-human accuracy.

tasks: Formulate clear instruction parameters to categorize user review feedback into precise operational categories.

sessions.title: Reasoning, Tools, and External Information
sessions.description: Examine how models chain thoughts, connect with external APIs, search webs, and utilize real-time databases (RAG).
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a major mental bottleneck for learners: the illusion that a language model is a self-contained, omniscient brain. Up to this point, students have seen models as closed systems that generate text purely from internal parameters trained on past data. To transition them into elite operators, we must break this illusion and introduce the concept of the "augmented" model. Use the whiteboard to draw a clear boundary line. On the left, label it "The Core Engine (Parametric Memory)"—fixed, frozen in time, and prone to guessing when it lacks facts. On the right, label it "The External World (Active Tools)"—live databases, search engines, and APIs. Explain that modern AI excels not just by knowing things, but by acting as an orchestrator that knows how to use tools. This shift from pure generation to tool orchestration is the foundation of modern agentic systems.

Now, introduce the mechanics of how a model actually uses a tool. Many students mistakenly believe there is a hidden, hard-coded magical link between the AI and Google or a database. Demystify this on the whiteboard by showing the "Tool Use Loop." Draw a three-step cycle: 1. The user asks a question requiring real-time info (e.g., "What is the stock price of Apple today?"). 2. The model recognizes its parametric knowledge is insufficient and generates a structured command, like a function call or a search query, instead of a direct answer. 3. The hosting system intercepts this command, executes the real-world search, and feeds the raw text results back into the model's prompt window. The model then reads this fresh context and synthesizes the final answer. Emphasize that the AI doesn't "click" buttons; it writes a request, a wrapper program runs it, and the AI reads the output. This is the core mechanism of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and API integration.

To make this concrete, walk through a step-by-step trace of a live search query. Show the difference between a system with "thought chaining" (like ReAct or Chain-of-Thought prompting) and one without. On the whiteboard, write out a real-world scenario where a user asks for a comparison of two recent, post-training events. Illustrate the model's inner monologue: "Thought: I need to find event A's date first. Action: Search[Event A date]. Observation: [Search returns Oct 12]. Thought: Now I need event B's date. Action: Search[Event B date]..." By visualizing this step-by-step thinking process, students understand that "reasoning" in AI is actually a sequential generation process where intermediate steps are used to plan subsequent tool calls. Address the common misconception that models do all this instantly in a single parallel flash; make it clear that it is highly iterative.

Introduce the hands-on practice block to expose the limitations and fragility of this loop: identifying "lookup gaps" and tool failures. Have the students analyze a pre-constructed, flawed trace where a model failed to answer a complex query because it formulated a bad search term or miscalculated the search results. Guide them to dissect where the breakdown happened. Did the model query the wrong keyword? Did the external search tool return irrelevant clutter? Or did the model fail to synthesize the correct answer from the retrieved context? This exercise teaches students that tool-use is a pipeline with multiple points of failure. By teaching them to debug these search traces, we equip them with the mental models needed to diagnose and optimize complex AI workflows in their own professional projects.

tasks: Deconstruct an AI response process that queries external search tools to identify lookup gaps.

lectures.title: AI's Limitations
lectures.description: Analyze key mathematical boundaries of prediction networks, specifically exploring errors, structural bias, and knowledge cliffs.

sessions.title: Why AI Hallucinates
sessions.description: Understand that hallucinations are logical, fluent next-token choices lacking factual search foundations or verification layers.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome back. Today we are tackling one of the most persistent and misunderstood phenomena in artificial intelligence: hallucinations. In a public-lecture format focused on conceptual clarity, our main objective is to shift the learner's perspective from viewing hallucinations as a random glitch or a temporary bug to understanding them as a direct, mathematical consequence of how next-token prediction works. We must dismantle the misconception that AI possesses an internal 'truth database' that it occasionally fails to query. Instead, we will draw a whiteboard schematic showing that generative networks only optimize for linguistic probability and logical flow, completely divorced from factual verification.

Let's start by sketching a simple sentence completion flow on the whiteboard. Write the phrase: 'The first person to walk on the moon was...' and draw a branching probability tree representing the model's choices. Show how 'Neil' receives the highest mathematical weight because of the vast amount of training data reinforcing this association. Now, contrast this by writing a prompt about a completely fictional event or a highly obscure, non-existent historical figure, such as: 'The academic contributions of Dr. Sarah Jenkins-Smith (born 1982) regarding the Martian Soil Treaty of 1998 are...'. On the board, draw the branching path for this prompt. Point out that the model does not have a 'fact-check' switch that says 'this person does not exist.' Instead, the network must generate the most linguistically plausible next words based on patterns of academic profiles. It will write fluent, highly convincing descriptions of publications, institutions, and research methodologies because those tokens flow naturally after the prompt. Explain to the audience that the model is doing exactly what it was trained to do: generating highly coherent, contextually appropriate language. It cannot distinguish between a factual memory and a plausible fabrication because to a mathematical prediction engine, both are simply paths of high probability.

Next, dive into the mechanics of why these fabrications look so incredibly convincing. On the whiteboard, map out a three-layer diagram representing the generation process: Syntax/Grammar at the bottom, Semantic Coherence in the middle, and Factual Grounding (marked with a large red 'X') at the top. Explain that modern LLMs are masters of syntax and semantic coherence—they know exactly how professional, authoritative text sounds. They mimic the structures of peer-reviewed papers, legal documents, and news articles perfectly. This is the source of the danger: the fluency of the output masks the complete absence of an underlying factual search engine. Warn the learners of a common pitfall: assuming that a confident tone implies factual correctness. A model does not feel 'doubt'; it merely calculates probabilities.

To solidify this intuition, we will conduct an interactive whiteboard exercise. We will write down a simulated, highly realistic-sounding explanation generated by an AI about a fabricated scientific concept (e.g., 'Retrograde Cellular Osmosis in Silicon-Based Plant Life'). As a class, we will systematically deconstruct this passage piece by piece. We will circle the terms that sound scientifically valid, highlight the logical connectors (like 'therefore' and 'as a result') that trick our brains into accepting the logic, and then point out the fatal flaw: the underlying physical premise is completely made up. This exercise will teach learners to look past structural fluency and look for independent verification. We will conclude by emphasizing that because sandboxed models lack live search or deterministic validation layers, they are generators of plausibility, not truth. To make them reliable, we must explicitly build verification workflows into our utilization strategies, which we will explore later in this unit.

tasks: Deconstruct a simulated hallucinated explanation, identifying the logical-sounding but factual inconsistencies.

sessions.title: Bias and Training Data
sessions.description: Analyze why systemic human stereotyping and skewed data distribution find their way directly into AI predictions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
To begin this whiteboard session, the teacher must dismantle the common misconception that AI is an objective, mathematical judge, free from human error. The whiteboard should start with a simple drawing of a clean pipeline: 'Raw World Data' flowing into a 'Machine Learning Box' and spitting out 'Predictions.' Draw a big, red question mark over the machine learning box. Explain that models do not learn from the world directly; they learn exclusively from records of the world, which are created, selected, and labeled by humans. If the historic records contain patterns of systemic inequality, underrepresentation, or skewed distributions, the model will treat these historically biased patterns as absolute mathematical truths. The core idea here is that optimization math is indifferent to ethics; it merely seeks to minimize prediction error against the training data it is given.

Next, visually unpack 'skewed distribution' or representation bias using a concrete, non-technical scenario on the whiteboard. Draw a simple bar chart representing a training dataset for an automated resume screening tool. Show a massive bar for 'Resume Data: Demographic Group A' alongside a tiny, almost invisible bar for 'Resume Data: Demographic Group B.' Walk students through the cascading mathematical consequences: because the model's loss function penalizes errors on the majority group much more heavily than on the minority group, the model will organically optimize its neural weights to excel at predicting success for Group A while discarding or misclassifying signals from Group B. The teacher should actively warn against the misconception that 'removing sensitive variables' (like gender or race labels) solves the problem. Illustrate on the board how other variables—such as zip codes, hobby clubs, or universities—act as proxies, allowing the model to easily reconstruct the excluded demographic information.

Transition the lecture into an active, whiteboard-driven debugging exercise. Present a hypothetical historical dataset of loan approvals spanning the last 40 years, where low-income neighborhoods were systematically denied credit. Ask students to identify how this historical bias becomes self-fulfilling: if the model is trained on this data, it will predict that applicants from these neighborhoods are high-risk. If banks use this model, they will deny loans, thereby preventing these neighborhoods from accumulating wealth, which in turn feeds 'bad' data back into the next generation of models. Draw this vicious feedback loop explicitly on the whiteboard to help students visualize the systemic compounding effect of algorithmic bias.

Finally, lead the students through a brainstorming session on how to balance these results, listing mitigation strategies directly on the whiteboard. Contrast 'pre-processing' techniques (such as oversampling minority groups or synthetic data generation) with 'in-processing' adjustments (like modifying the loss function to penalize unfairness) and 'post-processing' constraints (like shifting decision thresholds for different groups to ensure equal opportunity). Emphasize that resolving bias is not a one-click technical patch, but a continuous human-in-the-loop design choice that requires balancing mathematical tradeoffs between raw accuracy metrics and equitable performance across diverse populations.

tasks: Identify representation bias in a historical dataset and list strategies to balance model results.

sessions.title: Knowledge Limits and Missing Context
sessions.description: Define static cutoff dates, localized blindspots, and the absence of live physical reasoning in sandboxed networks.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by introducing the metaphor of the 'Frozen Library.' Explain that once a model's training phase is complete, its weights are locked in place, creating a hard temporal boundary known as the knowledge cutoff date. Illustrate this on the whiteboard as a physical vault door that was welded shut on a specific date. Learners often struggle to grasp that a highly conversational AI cannot 'just look up' this morning's news; the teacher must emphasize that without active external integration, the model's universe is entirely static. This sets up the fundamental reasoning limit: the system does not dynamically acquire new memories during a conversation.

Next, expand the whiteboard diagram to demonstrate what happens when a query goes past this temporal cliff. Draw a timeline showing the pretraining cutoff on one side and the present day on the other. Walk through a scenario where a user asks about a company merger that happened last week. Explain that because the model operates on next-token probability based on historic data, it will not experience an error crash; instead, it will confidently generate a response using pre-cutoff semantic associations, creating highly plausible but entirely outdated or incorrect assertions. This visual demonstration helps learners understand that the model's error is structural, not a temporary glitch.

Transition to the concept of sandboxed networks and the absence of physical reasoning. Draw a distinction on the board between 'linguistic knowledge' and 'grounded experience.' Explain that the model has never touched an object, experienced gravity, or witnessed spatial relationships. Its understanding of physics is purely statistical—knowing that the word 'drop' is frequently followed by 'fell to the floor.' Address the common student pitfall of assuming the model has a hidden simulation engine running in the background. Explain that without sensory grounding or real-time physical feedback, spatial puzzles or real-world planning tasks quickly expose the mathematical boundaries of pure text prediction.

Introduce the solution to these structural limits through the concept of 'Open-Book' versus 'Closed-Book' reasoning. On the left side of the whiteboard, sketch a student taking an exam with zero external materials—this represents standard model inference relying solely on static weights. On the right side, sketch the same student handed a specific reference document containing the exact answer—this represents context injection. Explain that by passing fresh, external data directly into the prompt window alongside the user query, we bypass both the static cutoff and the model's memory limitations by forcing the self-attention mechanism to focus on the provided text rather than old parameters.

Conclude with a structured prompt-crafting walkthrough on the whiteboard. Write out a template that explicitly isolates the 'Context' from the 'Instruction.' Show learners how to partition the prompt using clear delimiters (such as XML tags or triple quotes) to feed the model verified, real-time data. Explain the design choices behind adding constraints, such as 'Base your answer only on the provided text, and if the information is missing, state that you do not know.' This live prompt construction demonstrates to learners how to mathematically anchor the network's prediction focus, transforming a fragile knowledge-restricted system into a highly accurate context-driven processor.

tasks: Formulate a prompt structure that mitigates knowledge gaps by explicitly injecting updated external context.

lectures.title: Using AI Responsibly
lectures.description: Gain the practical security mindsets needed to handle intellectual assets and safety workflows safely.

sessions.title: Privacy and Sensitive Information
sessions.description: Understand system data leaks, user agreement rules, and which sensitive assets should never pass through public models.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome learners to this session on data privacy and security when using public artificial intelligence models. This session establishes a vital shift in perspective: from viewing AI as a private digital assistant to understanding it as a public, cloud-hosted computational processing engine. The primary goal is to demystify how data moves from a user's local input box into external training loops, helping learners realize that absolute trust in cloud systems is a security vulnerability. By framing this visually on our whiteboard, we will show that when you send data to a standard consumer LLM, that data does not simply vanish after generating an answer; instead, it travels through servers, becomes stored in logs, and may be used to train future iterations of the model.

To visualize this, draw a horizontal line across the whiteboard labeled the 'Trust Boundary.' Above this line is the local user environment (the user's computer, local memory, and private network). Below this line is the external cloud environment, containing the LLM provider's API endpoints, processing servers, and eventual cold-storage databases. Write a sample sentence at the top: 'Our company, Acme Corp, is planning to acquire BetaTech for $50 million in June, led by Director Jane Doe.' Explain that this sentence contains three distinct tiers of sensitive information: proprietary business strategy, specific financial figures, and personally identifiable information (PII). Walk through the journey of this sentence crossing the Trust Boundary. Once it falls below the line, the user loses physical custody. The LLM provider processes this data to generate a response, but unless explicit opt-outs or enterprise data processing agreements (DPAs) are active, this raw text resides in history logs where human reviewers or automated training pipelines can access it.

Address the common misconception that 'incognito mode' or simply deleting a chat from your history tab deletes the data from the provider's servers. Explain to the students that a chat history deletion often only removes the pointer from the user interface, while the raw API logs remain subject to the provider's standard data-retention policies. This is where we introduce the logic of proactive client-side redaction. Instead of hoping the model provider is secure, we must scrub sensitive parameters before they ever cross the Trust Boundary. Demonstrate this on the whiteboard by drawing a 'Redaction Filter' block right at the Trust Boundary. Show the process of transforming the previous sentence into: 'Our company, [Company A], is planning to acquire [Company B] for [Transaction Value] in [Timeline], led by [Director Title].' Explain that the structural meaning of the prompt remains fully intact, allowing the AI to draft an acquisition announcement or integration plan without ever knowing the real-world identity or values involved.

Now, initiate an active whiteboard audit simulation. Present raw, unredacted corporate emails, customer support transcripts, or software code containing API keys. Guide students through identifying what constitutes 'toxic input data'—such as personal emails, medical symptoms, exact revenue forecasts, or proprietary algorithms. Show them how to systematically substitute these elements with generic variables or functional placeholders. Emphasize that preserving semantic structure is the key; if you replace 'Jane Doe' with 'Noun,' the AI lose context, but replacing 'Jane Doe' with '[Lead HR Representative]' maintains the relationship mapping, allowing the AI to generate highly contextual, useful output while keeping sensitive details safe on the local side of the Trust Boundary.

tasks: Audit sensitive inputs and redact identifying data before passing text to an external web tool.

sessions.title: Checking Sources and Important Claims
sessions.description: Establish clear double-check practices to audit citations, critical computations, and output validation loops.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by addressing the dangerous illusion of authority that AI outputs project. Because LLMs generate text that is grammatically flawless and highly confident in tone, users naturally default to trusting them. In this session, the goal is to break that automatic trust and replace it with a systematic, adversarial verification mindset. We must explicitly teach students that an AI-generated citation, historical fact, or mathematical calculation is merely a 'prediction of what a correct answer looks like,' not an actual lookup of verified truth. 

To visualize this, the teacher will draw a 'Trust vs. Verification' matrix on the whiteboard. On one axis, we plot the criticality of the claim (e.g., a medical fact versus a creative brainstorming idea); on the other, we plot the source distance (whether the AI claims it came from a specific URL or just 'general knowledge'). The core teaching beat here is demonstrating how to isolate high-risk claims—specifically direct quotes, statistics, legal citations, and mathematical proofs—and isolate them for independent checking. 

Next, the teacher will walk through the anatomy of a hallucinated source. Often, a model will synthesize a real-sounding author name, a plausible journal title, and a fake DOI number that looks perfectly formatted but leads to a 404 page. The teacher should model a live 'structured lookup workflow' on the board. This workflow consists of three steps: isolating the claim, locating the primary source manually using external academic or general search engines, and matching the specific context of the source with the AI's claim. We emphasize that a student should never search for the full generated sentence, as search engines might feed into the same loop; instead, they must extract key entities and search for the actual primary document.

To solidify this, the session transitions into an active verification exercise. The teacher projects an AI-generated summary of a scientific study containing three citations and one mathematical calculation. The students' task is to act as truth-auditors. They will practice identifying which elements are highly suspicious, using a structured worksheet to run verification queries, and flagging mismatches. This exercise exposes a critical learner misconception: the belief that if two out of three citations are real, the third must be real too. By showing a case where the mathematical calculation is subtly off or one citation is completely fabricated, we install a healthy, permanent skepticism.

tasks: Verify the factual citations of an unverified output utilizing a structured lookup process.

units.title: Becoming a Smarter AI User
units.description: Transition from a passive bystander into a deliberate, skilled AI user. Master advanced prompt structuring, iteration methods, and rigorous model evaluation.

lectures.title: Communicating with AI
lectures.description: Learn functional prompt design principles, exploring structural clarity, constraints, and conversational formatting.

sessions.title: Giving Clear Instructions
sessions.description: Avoid vague queries. Master instructional precision by specifying role-play setups, explicit constraints, formats, and structural layouts.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by confronting the most common pitfall in human-AI interaction: treating the large language model like an intuitive human mind readers rather than a mathematical prediction engine. Most absolute beginners draft prompts that are vague, conversational, and open-ended, such as 'Write a blog post about productivity.' The teacher should illustrate on the whiteboard how this open-ended query forces the model to search a massive, unconstrained probability space, leading to generic, unhelpful, and cliché outputs. By drawing a wide, unfocused circle representing this vast space, we visually demonstrate how lack of specificity leads to 'average' answers.

To move from vague queries to structured commands, the teacher introduces the foundational concept of role-playing and framing. By defining a specific persona (e.g., 'You are an expert copywriter specializing in minimalist time-management systems'), we instantly narrow the probability space down to a targeted domain. The whiteboard should map this as a sharp funnel, narrowing the wide circle of all possible English outputs into a highly specialized subset of professional vocabulary, tone, and pacing. We explain that models do not possess an ego or self-identity; instead, they simulate patterns based on the context provided, making persona-setting a mathematical constraint rather than just a creative exercise.

Next, the teacher breaks down the anatomy of structural constraints and explicit layouts. A high-performing prompt requires a clear separation of instruction, input data, and output format. The teacher will sketch a template on the board using distinct delimiters like triple backticks (```) or XML-style tags (<instructions>, <context>, <constraints>) to show how the model distinguishes between what it must do and the data it must do it to. This structural scaffolding prevents the model from experiencing 'instruction drift'—a common misunderstanding where the model mistakenly processes user input text as a new set of instructions.

We then transition to a guided practice workspace. The teacher presents a poorly constructed, real-world conversational prompt: 'Help me draft an email to my team about a late project, make it sound professional and tell them what the new deadline is.' The learners are tasked with systematically converting this into a multi-part, structured directive. The teacher guides them to define the sender's exact role, establish strict formatting rules (such as bullet points for action items and a bolded bold date for the new deadline), and set explicit negative constraints (e.g., 'Do not use defensive language or passive-aggressive phrasing'). This exercise highlights the direct correlation between highly constrained instructions and predictable, high-quality, zero-draft outputs.

tasks: Rewrite vague conversational prompts into highly structured instructions with exact limits and constraints.

sessions.title: Providing Context and Examples
sessions.description: Master few-shot learning by injecting positive examples, structural output skeletons, and conversational context.
sessions.sessionOutline:
To begin this session, we must dismantle the naive assumption that a large language model implicitly understands the nuanced tone, structure, or categorization criteria we desire from a single-line instruction. This session focuses on the concept of 'few-shot learning'—the practice of feeding the model explicit input-output pairs to serve as a structural template. As a concept-first public lecture, we must visually demonstrate to the audience that instead of writing exhaustive rules to define a tone (which often fail), we can show the model what we want. On our virtual whiteboard, we draw a clear split: on the left side, we show a dry, unsuccessful zero-shot prompt trying to explain a complex sentiment classification task using wordy definitions; on the right side, we sketch out a clean, structured template with three concrete examples. This visual contrast immediately reveals that models are, at their core, pattern-replication engines. By seeing the repeating shape of the inputs and outputs, the model aligns its neural weight dynamics to mimic that exact pattern.

Next, the lesson dives into the anatomy of an effective few-shot example. We walk through the concept of 'structural output skeletons.' We show how formatting our examples using consistent delimiters (like 'Input: [text] \n Output: [label]') acts as a powerful guide. This is crucial because learners often make the mistake of using messy, inconsistent formats across their examples, which confuses the model's pattern matching. We explain that the examples we provide must cover diverse edge cases; if we are building a sentiment classifier for customer reviews, our three examples shouldn't all be simple 'happy' or 'angry' reviews. Instead, we should include a tricky, sarcastic review where the literal words are positive but the true sentiment is negative. This teaches the model the precise boundary lines of our task, turning a vague instruction into a highly accurate, context-aware system.

We then transition to an active practice moment, designed to expose a common misconception: that 'more examples are always better.' We challenge the learners to build a three-example 'few-shot' prompt template to guide an assistant on a highly subjective and tricky labeling task, such as separating constructive feature requests from general complaints. During this exercise, we guide them to realize that if their examples contain bias or inconsistent labeling, the model will faithfully replicate those errors. The goal of this practice is to show that quality, diversity, and structural consistency of context are far more important than the raw volume of examples. We wrap up by demonstrating how these contextual anchors drastically reduce 'hallucinations' by keeping the model's next-token predictions locked tightly within the structural framework we have defined.

tasks: Build a three-example 'few-shot' prompt template to guide an assistant on a tricky labeling task.

sessions.title: Improving an Answer Through Iteration
sessions.description: Ditch the one-and-done mindset. Master conversational loops, corrective prompts, style adjustments, and iterative critiques.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by confronting the single greatest psychological barrier that beginner AI users face: the 'one-shot search engine' mentality. Most people approach an AI model the same way they approach Google, typing a single query, looking at the initial output, and—if it is not perfect—concluding that the AI is incompetent. To dismantle this misconception, the teacher should draw a stark comparison on the whiteboard. On the left, draw a straight, single-arrow line representing the 'Search' model: Query leads directly to Result (and if the result is wrong, you must start over with a new query). On the right, draw a circular loop representing the 'Dialogue' model. This loop shows an initial prompt generating a rough draft, which is then fed back into the system with corrective feedback, leading to a refined draft. The core takeaway here is that an AI is not an oracle delivering final truths; it is a highly capable assistant that expects an editorial cycle.

Next, the teacher must explain *why* the first response is often underwhelming. Based on the statistical next-token prediction mechanisms discussed in previous units, a model's first unconstrained response is naturally going to lean toward the most average, statistically safe interpretation of the prompt. It is generic because it is trying to satisfy a broad probability distribution. To make the output outstanding, we must squeeze that distribution by applying successive constraints. The whiteboard should illustrate this as a funnel: the top of the funnel represents the wide, generic first draft, while each subsequent corrective prompt acts as a filter that narrows the focus, forcing the model to produce increasingly specific, high-quality text.

To bring this to life, the teacher will walk through a live, iterative scenario. Suppose we want to write a launch email for a local bakery's new sourdough bread. The teacher writes the initial lazy prompt on the board: 'Write an email about our new bread.' The resulting output is inevitably cheesy and stuffed with marketing clichés like 'delight your taste buds' and 'artisanal perfection.' Instead of throwing this draft away, the teacher demonstrates how to dissect it. We identify three flaws: it is too long, the tone is overly dramatic, and it ignores the actual unique selling points—like the 24-hour fermentation process and organic local flour. This analysis sets up our first corrective prompt.

Now, the teacher writes the corrective prompt on the board: 'This is too hyperbolic. Rewrite it to be warm but understated. Emphasize that we ferment the dough for 24 hours using local organic rye, and keep the total length under 150 words.' The teacher explains the logical chain here: we did not start over. We referenced the existing draft, named what we disliked (hyperbolic tone), specified what to retain or add (fermentation, rye), and added structural constraints (length). This shows the model how to pivot. A common pitfall for students here is opening a brand-new chat window to try again. The teacher must explicitly warn against this, explaining that continuing the current conversation is vital because the chat's 'context window' acts as a shared memory, keeping the draft and our critiques in its immediate view.

Finally, we introduce the concept of 'structural critiques' as an advanced iterative tactic. Instead of simply telling the model to 'make it better,' the teacher shows how to ask the model to analyze its own work. We write a prompt such as: 'Read the draft above. Point out three potential objections a customer might have regarding our pricing, and then revise the email to subtly address those objections.' This technique leverages the model's pattern recognition to self-correct before the final output is generated. For the active practice segment, the teacher will challenge learners to take a poorly written, robotic paragraph and use at least three successive, distinct follow-up prompts—focusing on tone shift, constraint addition, and structural reformulating—to transform it into a polished, natural piece of copy.

tasks: Refine a flawed initial draft output through successive corrective follow-up prompts.

lectures.title: Evaluating AI
lectures.description: Equip yourself to benchmark system performances objectively, selecting optimal platforms for actual use-cases.

sessions.title: Comparing Models and Responses
sessions.description: Establish scoring criteria (clarity, detail, safety) to objectively benchmark different models against one another.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by confronting a common pitfall: the 'vibe check' method of evaluating AI. Most users copy-paste a prompt, read the response, and declare a model 'good' or 'bad' based on a single subjective interaction. To move from passive technology observers to deliberate, competent AI operators, we must replace this casual impressionism with systematic, multi-dimensional benchmarking. The core concept to introduce here is that no single model is universally superior; instead, models represent different trade-offs in clarity, detail, safety, and alignment to specific constraints. By mapping out a physical whiteboard matrix, we will visually show how qualitative text can be decomposed into quantitative, actionable scores.

First, draw a grid on the whiteboard. The columns will represent competing models (for example, Model A and Model B), while the rows represent our primary evaluation dimensions: Clarity (Does it directly answer the prompt without fluff?), Detail (Is the depth of information appropriate for the target audience?), and Safety/Factuality (Are there hallucinated facts or boundary violations?). Explain to the students that these criteria are not arbitrary; they are the exact levers developers use to align models. For absolute beginners, illustrate this with an analogy: evaluating an AI is like hiring a contractor—you don't just ask if they are 'good'; you evaluate their speed, accuracy, and adherence to safety codes separately. 

Next, introduce a concrete scenario to anchor the evaluation. Imagine asking two different models to explain 'how a transformer neural network processes a word' to a non-technical manager. Present two simulated outputs. Model A provides a beautifully formatted, high-level summary with a brilliant spotlight analogy but glosses over the actual step of turning words into numbers. Model B provides a highly precise, step-by-step description of vector math but uses dense jargon that would alienate the target manager. Walk through the rubric step-by-step, showing how Model A scores high on clarity but lower on necessary detail, while Model B scores low on clarity for the specified audience but exceptionally high on raw detail.

Address a critical misconception: students often assume that the 'most detailed' answer is always the winner. We must explicitly point out that context dictates the rubric's weighting. If the target audience was a software engineer, Model B's profile is far superior. If the audience is a business executive, Model A wins. This realization shifts their mental model of AI from a search engine (which is either right or wrong) to a collaborative agent whose output must be fit-for-purpose.

Conclude the session with an interactive practice run where the students are handed a raw grading matrix and two competing responses to a customer complaint email. One response is overly empathetic but fails to offer a concrete refund solution; the other is blunt and transactional but solves the billing issue immediately. Guide the students to score these drafts against clarity, detail, and safety parameters. This practice reveals whether students can decouple their emotional reaction to an AI's 'tone' from its actual performance against specific operational criteria, solidifying their objective evaluation skills.

tasks: Evaluate and score two competing model outputs using a formal rubric matrix.

sessions.title: Testing AI on a Real-World Task
sessions.description: Walk through a workplace setup to deploy and test an AI workflow directly on real task parameters.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by clearing the whiteboard to draw a comprehensive architecture diagram of an AI Testing Pipeline. Emphasize to the learners that the biggest mistake organizations make is relying on a 'vibe check'—testing a prompt three times, seeing good results, and immediately deploying it. Explain that moving from amateur AI user to expert system builder requires a systematic, parameterized sandbox. On the whiteboard, draw a central node representing the 'System Under Test', with inputs flowing in from the left and an evaluative framework auditing outputs on the right.

Guide the students through mapping out the variables of a specific, high-stakes real-world task, such as an automated customer-support responder handling billing disputes. Use the whiteboard to split this task into measurable components: input variables (customer history, dispute reason, tone) and system configurations (model type, system prompt, temperature). Show how isolating these variables allows us to pinpoint exactly why an output fails. Point out that without isolating variables, a developer might waste hours rewriting a prompt when the issue was actually a high temperature setting causing erratic syntax.

Introduce the concept of a 'Golden Dataset' on the whiteboard. This is a hand-curated collection of test cases that represents the battlefield of real-world use. Instruct the teacher to visually partition this dataset into three distinct categories: Standard Cases (60%), Edge Cases (20%), and Adversarial Cases (20%). Explain that edge cases test structural limits (e.g., extremely long, disorganized inputs), while adversarial cases test safety boundaries (e.g., a customer trying to manipulate the AI into issuing an unauthorized refund). Explain that a test plan without adversarial cases is a liability waiting to happen.

Now, define the multi-dimensional evaluation rubric. Draw three distinct columns on the whiteboard: Technical Performance (latency, cost, token usage), Semantic Accuracy (factual alignment, adherence to company policy), and Behavioral Safety (avoidance of hallucinations, professional tone). Explain that a robust test plan must grade outputs against all three dimensions simultaneously. Illustrate a scenario where a prompt change improves accuracy by 5% but increases processing latency by 300%—demonstrating that optimization is always a series of trade-offs.

Conclude with an interactive whiteboarding exercise where students are presented with a mock output that successfully answered a customer query but violated an implicit safety policy by promising a delivery date before checking inventory. Walk the learners through logging this failure in a structured evaluation matrix, showing how to calculate an overall 'readiness score' for the model configuration.
